summary: Saudi Arabia and the Houthis trade strikes, Israel kills two Hamas officials, EU leaders weigh Ukraine money, US inflation rises, new US tariffs loom and China's AI labs slow.

question.text: The US is proposing tariffs on 14 economies, and new chip rules are slowing China's AI labs. For each policy, who inside the US gains and who pays, and how might the people paying try to change the outcome?

read.title: Russian casualties 'reach 450,000': What that means for the Ukraine war
read.summary: An explainer on leaked Russian death records: what they appear to show, who the dead are and where they came from, why the data is hard to verify, and what analysts think it means.

topics.heading: Houthis hit a Riyadh tower again as Saudi Arabia strikes Yemen's main port
topics.summary: Houthi drones struck the Saudi sovereign wealth fund's tower in Riyadh, injuring 11 people, and Saudi Arabia answered with a large strike on Yemen's Hodeidah port.[^1] Fires were then seen at the Ras Tanura oil complex; who caused them is not confirmed.[^1]

lead.title: Riyadh, Hodeidah and Ras Tanura Hit in Saudi-Houthi Exchange of Fire

alsoReported.title: Riyadh's tallest skyscraper hit in Houthi strike on Saudi wealth fund HQ

article: The Houthis are an armed movement backed by Iran that controls much of northern Yemen. Yemen's civil war, paused by a 2022 ceasefire, reignited in July during the wider US-Iran war, and the Houthis now hold Yemen's entire Red Sea coast.[^2] Saudi Arabia, which entered Yemen's war in 2015, leads a coalition against them.[^2]

On Tuesday, Houthi drones hit the PIF Tower in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District, home to Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund. Saudi civil defence says 11 people were injured, all foreign nationals.[^1] It was the second hit on that tower: a Houthi missile blew out windows on seven or eight floors on Nov 19, and an Aramco building nearby was hit on Nov 8.[^2][^1]

Saudi Arabia ordered Hodeidah, Yemen's largest commercial port and a key Houthi supply hub, to be evacuated, then struck it overnight. No damage or casualty figures had been released.[^1] Houthi leaders told people to leave Saudi Red Sea ports and threatened to strike back. Early Wednesday, Saudi forces reported a drone strike at Ras Tanura, one of the world's largest refining and oil-export sites; satellite and heat data show large fires, but responsibility has not been confirmed.[^1]

Why it matters: Saudi Arabia ships much of its oil from Ras Tanura, and the Red Sea is a main trade route between Asia and Europe. Reuters reported that Saudi officials expect the campaign to last up to six months and want gains on the ground before any talks.[^2]

My read: this is a second front of the Iran war that is getting closer to energy infrastructure. Watch whether the Houthis carry out their threat against ports such as Jeddah, and whether any outside mediator tries to separate the Yemen fight from the US-Iran talks.

topics.heading: Israel kills two Hamas security chiefs as Gaza declares a meningitis alert
topics.summary: Israeli strikes killed the head of Hamas's internal security and its northern Gaza chief on consecutive days; Palestinian outlets say the second strike also killed his wife and two daughters.[^3] Gaza's Health Ministry has issued an epidemic alert for meningitis.[^4]

lead.title: Israel kills second Hamas internal security chief in two days in IDF strike

alsoReported.title: Israeli air strikes in Gaza kill 7 as doctors warn of meningitis outbreak
Gaza Peace-Board Envoy Blames Netanyahu for Stalling Trump Deal

article: A ceasefire between Israel and Hamas has held, loosely, since October 2025, but strikes and deadly incidents continue. On Tuesday the Israeli military and the Shin Bet security service said they killed Naeem Abu Nahel, head of Hamas's internal security for the whole Gaza Strip.[^3] On Wednesday a strike on a home in Gaza City killed Muhammad Abu al-Ouf, Hamas's internal security chief for northern Gaza. Palestinian outlets reported that his wife and two daughters were also killed.[^3] Prime Minister Netanyahu and Defence Minister Katz praised what they called an "offensive policy".[^3]

Health is a second worry. Gaza's Health Ministry issued an epidemic alert for meningitis, an infection of the lining around the brain. A Gaza doctor told Al Jazeera there were 272 cases in October against a normal 30 to 50 a month, with 15 deaths so far this year.[^4] On Tuesday, strikes killed seven people in several parts of Gaza, according to local officials cited by Al Jazeera.[^4]

The bigger plan is stuck. Josh Gruenbaum, a senior adviser to the US-led Board of Peace that is meant to oversee Gaza's transition, publicly blamed Netanyahu for obstructing it.[^5] He said Israel has not signed an agreement for an international stabilisation force after more than six months, and vetted Palestinian police recruits are waiting for permission to train in Egypt. Netanyahu's office did not comment.[^5] About $18 billion in rebuilding aid depends on the plan moving forward.[^5]

What next: Israel is also between governments. Gadi Eisenkot has until Dec 6 to form a coalition. My read: the strikes and the political vacuum both make the next phase of the plan, including Hamas disarmament and an Israeli pullback, less likely to start soon.
topics.differences: Israel says it is targeting Hamas security commanders under the truce; Palestinian outlets report family members killed. A US-led board envoy blames Netanyahu for stalling the plan. Netanyahu's office did not comment on the envoy's criticism.[^3][^5]

topics.heading: EU leaders meet in Brussels on a 2028-2034 budget and a €45B loan for Ukraine
topics.summary: The 27 EU leaders begin a two-day summit on a seven-year budget that includes €100 billion for Ukraine, plus a new €45 billion loan for 2027.[^6] Diplomats expect a final deal only at next month's summit.[^6]

lead.title: EU leaders seek to bridge their differences and agree on a budget deal and a new loan for Ukraine

article: The European Union sets its budget seven years at a time. On Thursday its leaders began a two-day summit in Brussels to narrow their differences over the 2028 to 2034 budget, which could equal 1% to 1.2% of the bloc's gross national income.[^6] European Council President António Costa has proposed a version about 10% smaller than the European Commission's plan, plus a new EU-wide tax on digital advertising that could raise about €5 billion a year.[^6]

Members split into familiar camps. Germany, Austria, the Netherlands and Sweden, which pay in more than they get back, want to spend less. A group led by France and Italy defends farm money and funds for poorer regions, which make up about two-thirds of the budget.[^6]

Ukraine is the sharpest question. The draft sets aside €100 billion for Ukraine over seven years. Separately, leaders must decide on a €45 billion loan for 2027, €20 billion for the economy and €25 billion for the armed forces, which the Commission would borrow on markets.[^6] German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has threatened to block the budget without a shared commitment to Ukraine from every member, while Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia oppose using EU money for military aid.[^6]

Why it matters: Russian strikes on Ukraine's energy system and Black Sea trade are straining its finances, and US support has become less certain.[^6] Elections could also change the room: Spain votes on Sunday, and France, Italy and Poland vote next year.[^6] This is a judgment, but a deal on the Ukraine loan at December's summit would show whether Europe can carry more of the cost on its own.
topics.differences: Germany says the cost of supporting Ukraine must be shared by all members; four central European governments reject EU money for military aid; net payers and the cohesion group disagree on the budget's size.[^6]

topics.heading: US inflation runs hotter in October, making a December Fed rate hike near certain
topics.summary: The Fed's preferred inflation gauge rose to 3.8% a year in October, and core inflation to 3.3%, slightly above forecasts.[^7] Revised data show the US economy grew at a 4.3% annual rate in the third quarter.[^8]

lead.title: Fed's favored inflation gauge heats up, solidifying a rate hike in December, with more likely next year

alsoReported.title: US economy grew at a solid pace in third quarter, revised data shows

article: The US Federal Reserve, the central bank, tries to keep inflation near 2% a year, mainly by raising or lowering the interest rate banks charge each other. Its favourite measure of prices is called PCE, for personal consumption expenditures. On Wednesday, data showed PCE inflation rose to 3.8% in October from 3.6% in September.[^7] Core PCE, which leaves out food and energy because they jump around, rose to 3.3%, a little above the 3.2% economists expected.[^7]

The same day, a revised estimate showed the economy grew at a 4.3% annual rate from July to September, faster than in the first half of the year.[^8] A strong economy and rising prices together usually push a central bank to raise rates.

Fed officials have mostly settled on a December increase but disagree on its size, according to Yahoo Finance.[^7] Governor Christopher Waller said a quarter-point hike would need a signal of another in January, or else a half-point move. Governor Lisa Cook warned the Fed risks falling "behind the curve". New York Fed President John Williams argued against "dramatic action", noting that rate changes take one to two years to work fully.[^7]

Why it matters beyond the US: higher US rates tend to lift borrowing costs and the US dollar around the world, including for Canadian mortgages and businesses. The Fed decides on Dec 9. My read: the war-driven rise in energy prices is the main reason inflation has climbed, so oil prices and the Iran talks may matter as much as the Fed's own choices.

topics.heading: US proposes new tariffs of 15% to 40% on 14 economies, including China and the EU
topics.summary: The US Trade Representative found that factory overcapacity in 14 economies harms US commerce and proposed new tariffs, from 15% on the EU and Japan to 35% on Vietnam.[^9] Canada is not on the list; Mexico was left undecided.[^9]

lead.title: Section 301 Tariffs of 15 to 40 Percent Proposed on 14 Trading Partners

alsoReported.title: U.S. wants to accommodate Canada on sectoral tariffs, Trump trade czar says

article: A tariff is a tax on imported goods, paid when they enter a country. Section 301 is a US trade law that lets the government respond to foreign practices it judges unfair. After an investigation, the US Trade Representative (USTR) found that "structural excess capacity" in manufacturing in 14 economies, meaning factories built to produce far more than their markets need, is unreasonable and burdens US business.[^9]

The proposed rates are 15% for the EU, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan; 18% for Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand; 20% for China and Singapore; 25% for India; and 35% for Vietnam.[^9] Each has an alternate rate: higher if trade talks go badly, lower if a country signs a trade agreement with the US. China's could rise to 40%.[^9]

Some goods are exempt, including those already covered by other US tariffs on steel, aluminum, vehicles, lumber, medicines and semiconductors.[^9] The public can comment until Jan 5, a hearing is set for Jan 25, and no start date has been given.[^9]

Canada is not among the 14. Separately, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Wednesday that Washington wants a deal that "accommodates" Canada on steel, aluminum and autos, though sticking points remain.[^10]

My read: the proposal works as both a threat and a bargaining tool, since lower rates are offered to countries that make deals. Who pays is a real question: tariffs are paid by importers and often passed on to shoppers, at a time when US inflation is already rising.

topics.heading: New US chip rules slow China's AI labs, and Nvidia pauses Southeast Asia shipments
topics.summary: Reuters sources say new US limits on renting powerful chips abroad, and a push against copying US models, are delaying Chinese AI releases.[^11] Nvidia has told partners to stop shipping AI servers to four Southeast Asian countries, the FT reports.[^13]

lead.title: US chip curbs, distillation crackdown threaten Chinese AI model development, sources say

alsoReported.title: Nvidia halts chip shipments to South-East Asia amid US crackdown

article: Training a top AI model takes huge numbers of advanced chips, mostly designed by Nvidia. The US already bans selling the best ones to China, so Chinese firms have rented computing power in data centres abroad. A new US rule in force since Nov 19 requires a licence for Chinese firms using large amounts of that computing overseas, roughly the equivalent of 750 Nvidia H100 chips or more, and also requires licences for advanced chip shipments to several countries.[^11]

Reuters, citing people at the companies, reports the effects. Z.AI, also called Zhipu, missed the planned November launch of its largest model, which could slip to early 2027. Moonshot AI expects its six-month release cycle to stretch to a year or more.[^11] US labs are also pushing back on "distillation", training a model on another model's answers; Anthropic said in September it had seen about 200 million suspect exchanges linked to Chinese developers.[^11] One Chinese researcher told The Information: "We are done."[^12]
Chinese firms are adapting. MiniMax says it will speed up its use of chips from Huawei and Alibaba, and Alibaba's chief executive said domestic chips will "underpin all this training".[^11]

The rule is also hitting Southeast Asia. The National, citing the Financial Times, reports Nvidia told partners to stop shipping AI servers to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia while licences are sorted out; Dell and Supermicro have told customers their orders will not be authorised.[^13]

My read: the rule may widen the US lead for a while, but it also gives China a strong reason to build its own chips faster. These reports rely on unnamed sources, so the size of the delays is not yet certain.
topics.differences: Reuters' sources describe serious delays at Chinese labs; Chinese executives say domestic chips will fill the gap. Cloud operators say the licence process is unclear.[^11][^13]
